prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- Charging chesty women more for their bras doesn't win a lot of support, British retailer Marks & Spencer acknowledged Friday as it announced an end to the surcharge on its larger lingerie. Marks & Spencer have apologised for charging chesty women more for bras. "We boobed," screamed a full-page Marks & Spencer ad, which appeared in British newspapers Friday. Marks & Spencer gave in to campaigners who argued that the higher prices of the bigger bras was unfair. The retailer charged as much as £2 ($3) more for all sizes DD and up. "It's true that our fantastic quality larger bras cost more money to make, and we felt it was right to reflect this in the prices we charged," the ad said. "Well, we were wrong." It follows a nearly year-long campaign by members of the Facebook group Busts 4 Justice. The women behind the site argued other chain retailers didn't charge extra for bigger sizes, so Marks & Spencer shouldn't, either. And it pointed out that the store doesn't charge extra for larger sizes of clothing, so it shouldn't charge more for larger undergarments. What's your view? "We would like to thank everyone who has supported us on this issue; especially the thousands of brilliant, busty women that have joined forces with us. We couldn't have done this without you," the two administrators of the group, Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, posted Friday on Facebook. "Busts 4 Justice remain committed to making things better for busty women on the high street, but for now we're happy just to be able to encourage all ladies to reward themselves and their boobs with some properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie." Marks & Spencer is a stalwart British chain, known for classic wardrobe staples and low prices. Its underwear department is the first stop for many British shoppers and is especially famous for reliable basics. And to give customers an added lift, Marks & Spencer also announced it is cutting the prices of all of its bras by 25 percent for the rest of May. "I think even though we all obviously held a bit of a grudge against buying our bras from M&S we should really be grateful they got rid of the surcharge and have given us the super generous 25 percent off," Mount wrote on the group's site Friday. "They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!"

“We boobed,” declared a full-page Marks & Spencer advertisement published in British newspapers on Friday.

The company reversed its position after pressure from campaigners who said the price difference was discriminatory. Bras in cup sizes DD and above had cost up to £2 ($3) more.

The advertisement explained that larger bras cost more to manufacture because of their high quality and that the retailer had initially believed its prices should reflect those additional expenses. “Well, we were wrong,” it concluded.

The decision came after an almost year-long effort by members of the Facebook group Busts 4 Justice. The campaigners noted that other major retailers did not impose extra charges for larger cup sizes and argued that Marks & Spencer should follow the same practice. They also pointed out that the company did not increase prices for larger clothing sizes, so it should not do so for bigger underwear.

What do you think?

On Friday, the group’s administrators, Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, thanked everyone who had backed the campaign, particularly the thousands of “brilliant, busty women” who had united behind it. They said the victory would not have been possible without that support.

They added that Busts 4 Justice would continue working to improve the shopping experience for fuller-busted women on Britain’s high streets. For the moment, however, they were pleased to encourage women to treat themselves—and their breasts—to properly fitted lingerie at fair prices.

Marks & Spencer is a long-established British retailer recognized for affordable prices and traditional wardrobe essentials. Many shoppers in Britain turn first to its lingerie section, which has a strong reputation for dependable basics.

The company also offered customers another boost by reducing the price of every bra by 25 percent for the remainder of May.

Writing on the group’s website Friday, Mount said that although campaigners had understandably been reluctant to buy bras from Marks & Spencer, they should appreciate both the removal of the surcharge and the retailer’s “super generous” 25 percent discount. She predicted that the stores might be sold out by the end of the weekend.

# Marks & Spencer drops surcharge on larger bras after Facebook campaign

**LONDON, England** — British retailer Marks & Spencer has announced it will stop charging an extra £2 for bras in sizes DD and above following pressure from an online campaign called Busts 4 Justice.

The campaign, launched on Facebook by shopper Beckie Williams, attracted thousands of supporters who argued that women with larger busts should not have to pay more for their underwear.

Marks & Spencer had previously defended the surcharge, saying larger bras required additional material and more complex construction. But the company reversed its position after growing criticism from customers.

In newspaper advertisements acknowledging the change, the retailer admitted: “We boobed,” and said all bras would now be sold under a single-price policy, regardless of cup size.

“We always try to do the right thing by our customers, and we’ve heard what they’re telling us,” the company said.

Williams welcomed the decision, describing it as a victory for consumers and for women who had long viewed the charge as unfair.

Marks & Spencer, one of Britain’s biggest lingerie retailers, also announced a temporary 25% discount on bras to accompany the policy change.

The Busts 4 Justice campaign highlighted the growing power of social media to organize customers and pressure major companies into changing pricing practices.

# M&S says ‘We boobed’ as campaign forces U-turn on larger-bra surcharge

**LONDON — Marks & Spencer has abandoned its policy of charging more for larger-cup bras after a campaign by shoppers accused the retailer of penalising women for the size of their breasts.**

The high-street chain announced that bras in DD cups and above would be sold at the same price as smaller sizes, reversing a policy under which some larger bras cost an additional £2.

The decision followed sustained pressure from Busts 4 Justice, a campaign founded by Beckie Williams that gathered about 13,000 supporters online. Activists argued that the surcharge was unfair because women had no choice over their bra size and should not be required to pay what campaigners described as a “boob tax”.

Williams and fellow supporters took their protest directly to Marks & Spencer, presenting the company with evidence of the strength of public opposition. The campaign made extensive use of Facebook and attracted national attention, turning a relatively small retail price difference into a wider argument about body shape, fairness and the treatment of female customers.

“I’m ecstatic,” Williams said after the company confirmed its change of policy. “I never thought it would happen. I just wanted to show them how many people disagreed with them.”

Marks & Spencer initially defended the higher prices on the grounds that larger bras required additional fabric, stronger components and more complicated construction. Sir Stuart Rose, then the company’s executive chairman, said the garments involved extra work and expense.

“We do charge more for big bras,” Rose said before the reversal. “The reasons are very simple. Bigger bras need more technology. They need more material, they need more work.”

At that stage, the retailer appeared determined to resist the campaign. But the activists maintained that the company’s argument did not justify singling out larger-busted women, particularly when many other garments were sold at a standard price across a range of sizes.

The pressure eventually prompted a conspicuous change of tone. In newspaper advertisements announcing the decision, Marks & Spencer admitted: **“We boobed.”**

The company said: “We listened to our customers. From Saturday, no matter what size you buy, the price will be the same.”

Marks & Spencer also offered a temporary 25 per cent discount on bras as part of the announcement, presenting the move as an effort to rebuild goodwill with customers.

The reversal was a significant victory for Busts 4 Justice, which had begun as a grassroots consumer protest rather than a large, professionally organised campaign. Its rapid growth demonstrated how social media could allow customers to coordinate pressure against a major national retailer.

Campaigners said the issue was about more than £2. For women who regularly bought several bras, the surcharge could accumulate, but activists also objected to the principle that customers with larger breasts were being treated differently.

The campaign’s message resonated partly because Marks & Spencer has long been one of Britain’s best-known underwear retailers. Its position in the lingerie market meant that its pricing decisions affected a large number of women and carried influence across the wider retail industry.

By ending the surcharge, the company sought to turn a public-relations setback into evidence that it was willing to respond to shoppers. Marks & Spencer said it was pleased to offer larger-busted customers better value, while acknowledging that its previous approach had caused considerable frustration.

For Williams and her supporters, the announcement vindicated a campaign built through petitions, online organising and direct action. What began as a complaint over a small price premium had forced one of Britain’s biggest retailers to reconsider a national pricing policy — and to concede, in its own words, that it had “boobed.”

## M&S scraps DD-plus bra surcharge after Facebook campaign

Marks & Spencer has abolished its £2 surcharge on bras in sizes DD and above after a Facebook-led protest accused the retailer of penalising women for having larger busts.

The high-street chain acknowledged its reversal with advertisements declaring: “We boobed.” From Saturday, May 9, bras of the same style will cost the same regardless of cup size.

As an apology—and a publicity push to mark the change—M&S will also cut the price of all bras by 25% for two weeks, from May 9 to May 23.

The U-turn follows pressure from Busts 4 Justice, a campaign launched on Facebook by customer Beckie Williams. The group attracted thousands of supporters and organised a protest outside the retailer’s flagship Marble Arch store in London.

Campaigners argued that the surcharge was discriminatory and unfair, saying women do not choose their bra size and should not have to pay more for essential support. They also questioned why larger cup sizes incurred an extra charge when many other garments were sold at a standard price across a range of sizes.

M&S had defended the policy on the grounds that DD-plus bras require additional fabric and more complex construction, including reinforced cups, wider straps and stronger fastenings. The company maintained that the £2 premium reflected higher production costs rather than an attempt to profit from larger-busted customers.

But the technical explanation failed to settle the wider fairness argument. For campaigners, the issue became less about the amount of money than the principle of charging one group of women more for the same design.

By dropping the surcharge, M&S has turned a potentially damaging dispute into a conspicuous apology. The May sale is likely to bring shoppers back into its lingerie departments, but the victory belongs largely to consumers who used social media to transform a niche complaint into a national retail debate.
